az_southern_arizona.blurb: Southern Arizona wraps around Tucson and the sky-island ranges that ring it, with climbing spread from low desert foothills up into pine forest. The Santa Catalina range above town holds by far the largest share, and Cochise Stronghold to the southeast adds remote domes and towers. Sport routes are the most common, trad is close behind, and bouldering makes up a solid share, plus a few top-ropes. Most climbs fall between 5.9 and 5.12, with the busiest band around 5.10 to 5.11 and a fair supply of easier lines. Rock is mostly granite and gneiss, with limestone and conglomerate in small pockets. Because elevation changes so much, there is always a cooler or warmer wall to chase: low crags suit winter, while the high mountain walls stay comfortable in summer. Expect real hiking to the best backcountry walls.

ca_lake_tahoe.blurb: The Tahoe region covers the high Sierra Nevada around the lake and the highway corridors that cross it, from the Truckee River side down to Carson Pass. Granite dominates, fine-grained and sticky, though a few volcanic crags such as basalt columns break the pattern. Bouldering is the largest category, followed by trad and sport, with a sprinkling of top-rope and a handful of scrambles and alpine objectives. Boulder problems run from easy to very hard, with plenty at the moderate end. Roped climbs mostly sit between 5.9 and 5.12, with a wide spread of easier routes too. The big corridors, I-80 and Highway 50, hold the most climbs, with the South Shore and West Shore next. Fall is prized for friction and cool air, spring and summer work well at different elevations, and winter is limited to lower, drier spots.

va_southwest_virginia_appalachia.blurb: Far southwestern Virginia is a patchwork of mountain parks, river gorges and boulder fields along the Appalachian ridges near the Tennessee, Kentucky and North Carolina lines. Bouldering dominates by a wide margin, with a smaller body of sport routes and a thin layer of trad. Problems run from very easy up through the hard grades, with the bulk in the low to middle range. Roped climbing is mostly 5.10 to 5.12, with some moderates. Sandstone is the main rock, with gneiss and quartzite in a few areas. Grayson Highlands is the big boulder destination, and its high elevation keeps summers tolerable. Guest River Gorge, Breaks Interstate Park and High Knob offer cliff and boulder sandstone at lower elevations. Spread across many small, scattered areas, it rewards a trip with a flexible plan.

az_northern_arizona.blurb: Northern Arizona stretches across the Colorado Plateau and Mogollon Rim, with Flagstaff, Sedona, Oak Creek Canyon and Sycamore Canyon as hubs, plus far-flung areas toward Kingman, Winslow and the Grand Canyon. The mix is unusually varied: trad slightly leads, sport follows closely, and bouldering is a sizable third. Most roped climbs fall between 5.9 and 5.13, concentrated at 5.10 to 5.12, with fewer easy routes. The rock changes with the town: limestone around Flagstaff and Winslow, sandstone in Sedona and Oak Creek, and volcanic basalt and dacite in other pockets. Sedona stone can be crumbly, so crack skills and care help. Flagstaff's cooler elevation draws climbers in summer, while lower walls and sunny limestone canyons suit winter. Distances between areas are long.

nv_red_rocks.blurb: Red Rock Canyon sits just west of Las Vegas, where a long escarpment of colorful sandstone rises out of the Mojave desert. The stone is porous and crumbly when wet, while the dark varnished faces are firmer and often the hardest. Trad is the most common style, with bouldering and sport nearly equal behind it. Grades run widely, from easy slabs to 5.13 and 5.14, but the heart of the area sits between 5.7 and 5.12, so moderates are plentiful. The sport-heavy crags cluster around Calico Basin and the Sandstone Quarry, while Pine Creek, Black Velvet and First Creek canyons offer long multi-pitch lines and crack climbing, and some walls need a real hike. Spring and fall are the favorites, winters are cold but workable, and summers are punishing.

co_south_platte.blurb: The South Platte is a broad swath of granite southwest of Denver, spread over foothill ridges, forested canyons and state park land rather than one crag. Sport climbs lead slightly, trad is nearly as big, and bouldering adds a notable share, with a few top-ropes. Roped grades span 5.5 to 5.13, with the thickest band around 5.9 to 5.12, so there are good moderates and hard projects alike. Devil's Head is a sport-focused area with fine-grained granite, roofs, cracks and edges, and a practical season from spring to late fall. Elevenmile Canyon runs along a river with long multi-pitch lines on solid granite and is workable most of the year. Areas are scattered, often on forest roads, so expect driving between them and a camp-style feel.
